objectives.text: Distinguish nutrition, health and disease, and say why health is more than the absence of disease.
Name the six classes of nutrients and say which three yield energy, and how much.
Explain what nutrient density measures and why it is not the same as calorie count.
Explain why an observational study cannot establish that a food causes an outcome.
Describe how genetics, environment, life stage and lifestyle each act on health status.

terms.gloss: A substance in food the body uses to grow, maintain itself and run its processes.
One the body cannot make in sufficient quantity, so it has to come from the diet.
A nutrient needed in large amounts: carbohydrate, lipid, protein and water.
A nutrient needed in small amounts: vitamins and minerals. Small amount, not small importance.
Essential nutrients per unit of energy. A food can be calorie-dense and nutrient-poor at the same time.
Observes populations as they are. It can show association; it cannot by itself show cause.

questions.prompt: How many of the six classes of nutrients yield energy?
options: Three — carbohydrate, lipid and protein
Four — carbohydrate, lipid, protein and water
Two — carbohydrate and lipid
Six — all of them
questions.why: Carbohydrate, lipid and protein yield energy. Water is a macronutrient because it is needed in large amounts, but it yields none; vitamins and minerals yield none either.
distractorNotes: Water is needed in large amounts but supplies no energy.
Protein yields energy too, at 4 kcal per gram.
Vitamins, minerals and water supply no energy.

questions.prompt: Which set of energy values per gram is right?
options: Carbohydrate 4, protein 4, lipid 9
Carbohydrate 9, protein 4, lipid 4
Carbohydrate 4, protein 9, lipid 4
Carbohydrate 7, protein 7, lipid 7
questions.why: Fat is the most energy-dense at 9 kcal per gram, more than twice carbohydrate or protein at 4.
distractorNotes: Reverses fat and carbohydrate.
Puts the high value on protein instead of fat.
Alcohol is 7 kcal per gram, but it is not one of the six nutrient classes.

questions.prompt: A food is high in calories but supplies few vitamins and minerals. How is that described?
options: Low nutrient density
High nutrient density
Low energy density
High fibre density
questions.why: Nutrient density is essential nutrients relative to energy. Plenty of energy with few nutrients is a low ratio.
distractorNotes: That would be many nutrients for few calories — the opposite.
Describes a person's status, not a property of the food.
The food is energy-rich, not energy-poor.

questions.prompt: A study finds people who eat more yogurt have lower rates of type 2 diabetes. What does that design support?
options: An association between yogurt intake and diabetes rates
A mechanism by which yogurt lowers fasting blood glucose
Evidence that yogurt prevents the onset of type 2 diabetes
Evidence that diabetes impairs the digestion of dairy sugar
questions.why: Observational data show association. Cause needs a design that controls what people consume and rules out confounders — overall diet quality, activity, income.
distractorNotes: A mechanism claim; this design measured neither blood glucose nor an intervention.
A causal-prevention claim, which observation alone cannot support.
Reverses the direction and adds digestion, which was not measured.

questions.prompt: Which design is best placed to show that a nutrient causes an effect?
options: A randomized clinical intervention trial
A much larger epidemiological cohort study
A population survey with a high response rate
A detailed case report on a single patient
questions.why: Randomizing who receives the intervention is what separates the nutrient from everything else that travels with it in real diets.
distractorNotes: Scale improves precision, not the ability to infer cause.
Still observational, however well sampled.
A single case can raise a question; it cannot settle one.

questions.prompt: The WHO definition of health is best summarised as:
options: Complete physical, mental and social health
Simply the absence of diagnosed disease
Normal results across a standard blood panel
Capacity to do a day's work without pain
questions.why: Health is defined positively and across three dimensions. Disease affects all three, which is why the definition is not simply its negation.
distractorNotes: This is the 'merely the absence of disease' phrasing the definition rejects.
Too narrow, and physical only.
Functional capacity is part of it, not the whole of it.

questions.prompt: Nutrients can change the way genes are expressed. What follows?
options: Genetic risk is modifiable rather than fixed at birth
Genetic inheritance has little bearing on disease risk
Dietary change can rewrite the underlying DNA sequence
Only conditions that are inherited will respond to diet
questions.why: Traits emerge from genes and environment together, and diet is part of the environment acting on expression.
distractorNotes: Overcorrects: genes do determine traits, including risk.
Expression changes; the underlying sequence does not.
Diet bears on risk broadly, not only inherited conditions.

questions.prompt: Which is a socioeconomic determinant of food choice rather than a biological one?
options: What food is affordable and reachable nearby
Life stage, such as pregnancy or adolescence
An inherited deficiency of the lactase enzyme
Resting metabolic rate and body composition
questions.why: Cost and access are environmental determinants, and they constrain choice regardless of what someone knows about nutrition.
distractorNotes: Life stage is biological, though it does change needs.
An inherited trait.
A physiological measure.

questions.prompt: Why does good nutrition count as health promotion rather than only disease prevention?
options: It builds well-being, not only avoidance of illness
Promotion and prevention describe the same activity
It removes the need for routine medical care
Its value only begins once disease appears
questions.why: Promotion works toward the positive state the definition of health describes; prevention works against a specific outcome. Nutrition does both.
distractorNotes: They are related but distinct ideas.
It reduces risk; it does not replace care.
Backwards — its value is largely before disease.

questions.prompt: Two of the six nutrient classes are needed in smaller amounts. Which?
options: Vitamins and minerals
Protein and water
Carbohydrate and lipid
Lipid and minerals
questions.why: Vitamins and minerals are micronutrients — needed in small amounts, essential all the same.
distractorNotes: Both are macronutrients.
Both are macronutrients.
Lipid is a macronutrient.

checklist: Name the two foods and give kcal per 100 g for each.
Say which is more energy dense and why, in terms of water and fat content.
Say what that means for how full you feel at equal volume.
selfCheck: Did I define energy density before using the phrase?
Did I give a number rather than 'more' or 'less'?
Is my comparison at equal weight or equal volume, and did I say which?

checklist: List grams of carbohydrate, protein and fat.
Add them and compare with the label's stated calories.
If the numbers differ, say why — rounding, fibre, or alcohol.
selfCheck: Did I use 9 for fat, not 4?
Does my total land within a few kcal of the label?
